title: Die zertanzten Schuhe
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 133. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, Thür, Rath, that, thaten, thun, gethan). The 1857 edition prints this tale without paragraph breaks; the paragraphing here is editorial, added for readability. The wording is unchanged.
about: KHM 133 tells of twelve princesses who are locked into their shared bedroom each night, yet whose shoes are found danced to pieces every morning; suitors who try to solve the mystery and fail are executed, until a poor soldier, aided by a cloak of invisibility and a warning against a drugged nightly drink, follows the princesses down through a trapdoor to an underground kingdom and its silver, gold, and diamond avenues.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der hatte zwölf Töchter, eine immer schöner als die andere.
sentences.l: There was once a king, who had twelve daughters, each one always fairer than the next.
sentences.i: There was once a king who had twelve daughters, each one fairer than the last.
sentences.n: “eine immer schöner als die andere” is a set formula for a row of sisters — literally ‘one always fairer than the other,’ which cannot be true of all of them at once and is not meant to be. The 1857 book runs this tale from beginning to end as a single paragraph; the breaks here are ours, put in for readability alone, and the German itself is untouched.

sentences.t: Sie schliefen zusammen in einem Saal, wo ihre Betten neben einander standen, und Abends, wenn sie darin lagen, schloß der König die Thür zu und verriegelte sie.
sentences.l: They slept together in one hall, where their beds stood beside one another, and in the evening, when they lay in them, the king shut the door to and bolted it.
sentences.i: They slept together in one great chamber, where their beds stood side by side; and in the evening, once they were lying in them, the king shut the door and bolted it.
sentences.n: “schloß … zu” is separable zuschließen, ‘to lock up’ — and “schloß” is spelled exactly like das Schloß, ‘castle,’ which turns up later as a noun. “Saal” is a large hall rather than a bedroom. “Thür” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern Tür).

sentences.t: Wenn er aber am Morgen die Thüre aufschloß, so sah er daß ihre Schuhe zertanzt waren, und niemand konnte herausbringen wie das zugegangen war.
sentences.l: But when he unlocked the door in the morning, he saw that their shoes were danced to pieces, and no one could find out how that had come about.
sentences.i: But when he unlocked the door in the morning, he saw that their shoes had been danced to pieces, and nobody could discover how it had happened.
sentences.n: “zertanzen” belongs to the family of German verbs in zer-, which means doing a thing until what you do it to falls apart: to dance a shoe to bits. English has no one verb for it, and the tale is named after the participle. “herausbringen” here is to get a thing out of someone, to find it out; “zugehen” is to happen, to come about.

sentences.t: Da ließ der König ausrufen wers könnte ausfindig machen, wo sie in der Nacht tanzten, der sollte sich eine davon zur Frau wählen und nach seinem Tod König sein:
sentences.l: Then the king had it proclaimed: whoever could find out where they danced in the night, he should choose one of them for a wife and be king after his death:
sentences.i: Then the king had it cried abroad that whoever could find out where they danced at night should choose one of them for his wife and be king after his death:
sentences.n: “wählen” here is the plain High German verb ‘to choose’; it governs “sich eine … zur Frau,” to choose one for oneself as a wife. “ausrufen lassen” is to have a thing proclaimed by a town crier. “ausfindig machen” lives only inside this phrase, ‘to find out, discover.’

sentences.t: wer sich aber meldete und es nach drei Tagen und Nächten nicht heraus brächte, der hätte sein Leben verwirkt.
sentences.l: but whoever presented himself and did not bring it out after three days and nights, he would have forfeited his life.
sentences.i: but whoever came forward and did not bring it to light within three days and nights would have forfeited his life.
sentences.n: “sich melden” is to come forward, to present oneself as a candidate. “sein Leben verwirken” is a legal phrase — to forfeit one’s life by one’s own act. “brächte” and “hätte” are subjunctive because the proclamation is being reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so meldete sich ein Königssohn und erbot sich das Wagnis zu unternehmen.
sentences.l: Not long, and a king’s son came forward and offered himself to undertake the venture.
sentences.i: It was not long before a king’s son came forward and offered to take the hazard on.
sentences.n: “nicht lange, so …” is a compressed narrative formula: ‘it was not long before.’ “sich erbieten” is to offer oneself for something. “Wagnis” is a venture with risk in it, built on wagen, to dare.

sentences.t: Er ward wohl aufgenommen, und Abends in ein Zimmer geführt, das an den Schlafsaal stieß.
sentences.l: He was well received, and in the evening led into a room that adjoined the sleeping-hall.
sentences.i: He was well received, and in the evening led into a room adjoining the sleeping hall.
sentences.n: “stieß” here is from anstoßen, ‘to abut on, adjoin,’ not the everyday stoßen, ‘to knock.’ “ward” is the older preterite of werden and builds the passive all through these tales.

sentences.t: Sein Bett war da aufgeschlagen und er sollte Acht haben wo sie hingiengen und tanzten;
sentences.l: His bed was made up there, and he was to take heed where they went and danced;
sentences.i: His bed was made up there, and he was to keep watch where they went and danced;
sentences.n: “ein Bett aufschlagen” is to set a bed up — the same verb as pitching a tent. “Acht haben” is to pay heed. “hingiengen” is the 1857 spelling of hingingen, from hingehen.

sentences.t: und damit sie nichts heimlich treiben konnten oder zu einem andern Ort hinaus giengen, war auch die Saalthüre offen gelassen.
sentences.l: and so that they could get up to nothing in secret, or go out to some other place, the hall door had also been left open.
sentences.i: and so that they could get up to nothing in secret, or slip out by some other way, the hall door had been left open as well.
sentences.n: “etwas treiben” is to get up to something, to carry it on — not the ‘drive a flock’ sense the same verb has elsewhere. “damit … konnten” is a purpose clause. “Saalthüre” is Saal plus Thüre in the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: Dem Königssohn fiels aber wie Blei auf die Augen und er schlief ein, und als er am Morgen aufwachte waren alle zwölfe zum Tanz gewesen, denn ihre Schuhe standen da und hatten Löcher in den Sohlen.
sentences.l: But it fell on the king’s son’s eyes like lead and he fell asleep, and when he woke in the morning all twelve had been at the dance, for their shoes stood there and had holes in the soles.
sentences.i: But it came down on the king’s son’s eyes like lead, and he fell asleep; and when he woke in the morning all twelve had been at the dance, for their shoes stood there with holes in the soles.
sentences.n: “dem Königssohn fiels … auf die Augen” is the dative of the person with the accusative of the part: it fell on his eyes. “fiels” is fiel es. Nothing is said yet about the wine — the reader is left to work out afterwards what the weight on his eyes was.

sentences.t: Den zweiten und dritten Abend giengs nicht anders, und da ward ihm sein Haupt ohne Barmherzigkeit abgeschlagen.
sentences.l: The second and third evening it went no otherwise, and then his head was struck off without mercy.
sentences.i: The second and third evening went no differently, and then his head was struck off without mercy.
sentences.n: “den zweiten und dritten Abend” is an accusative of time. “giengs” is gieng es (1857 for ging es). The sentence is as brief as the execution; the tale does not linger over it and the translation does not either.

sentences.t: Es kamen hernach noch viele und meldeten sich zu dem Wagestück, sie mußten aber alle ihr Leben lassen.
sentences.l: There came afterwards still many and put themselves forward for the hazard, but they all had to leave their lives.
sentences.i: Many more came afterwards and offered themselves for the hazard, but every one of them had to give up his life.
sentences.n: “sein Leben lassen” is the standing phrase for dying, ‘to leave one’s life.’ “Wagestück” is a piece of daring, close in sense to the Wagnis of a few lines back. “hernach” is an old word for afterwards.

sentences.t: Nun trugs sichs zu, daß ein armer Soldat, der eine Wunde hatte und nicht mehr dienen konnte, sich auf dem Weg nach der Stadt befand, wo der König wohnte.
sentences.l: Now it came to pass that a poor soldier, who had a wound and could serve no longer, found himself on the road to the town where the king lived.
sentences.i: Now it came to pass that a poor soldier, who had a wound and could serve no longer, was on the road to the town where the king lived.
sentences.n: “sich zutragen” is ‘to come to pass’; “trugs sichs” doubles the pronoun the way spoken German does. “sich befinden” is to be somewhere. A discharged soldier with a wound and no trade is a standing figure in these tales — the man with nothing left to lose.

sentences.t: Da begegnete ihm eine alte Frau, die fragte ihn wo er hin wollte.
sentences.l: There an old woman met him, who asked him where he wanted to go.
sentences.i: There an old woman met him, and asked him where he was bound.
sentences.n: “begegnen” takes the dative — literally ‘to him an old woman met.’ “wo er hin wollte” splits the compound wohin and lets wollen carry the going: ‘where he wanted to go.’

sentences.t: „Ich weiß selber nicht recht,“ sprach er, und setzte im Scherz hinzu „ich hätte wohl Lust ausfindig zu machen wo die Königstöchter ihre Schuhe vertanzen, und darnach König zu werden.“
sentences.l: “I do not rightly know myself,” he said, and added in jest, “I should rather like to find out where the king’s daughters dance their shoes away, and to become king after that.”
sentences.i: “I hardly know myself,” he said, and added as a joke, “I should not mind finding out where the king’s daughters dance their shoes away, and being king afterwards.”
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb wissen, ‘I know,’ not the adjective weiß, ‘white.’ “setzte … hinzu” is separable hinzusetzen, ‘to add.’ “Lust haben zu” is to feel like doing a thing. “darnach” is the 1857 spelling of danach.

sentences.t: „Das ist so schwer nicht,“ sagte die Alte, „du mußt den Wein nicht trinken, der dir Abends gebracht wird, und mußt thun als wärst du fest eingeschlafen.“
sentences.l: “That is not so hard,” said the old woman, “you must not drink the wine that is brought you in the evening, and must act as if you were fast asleep.”
sentences.n: “thun als” is to do as if, to pretend, and “wärst” is the subjunctive that als calls for. “die Alte” is an adjective used as a noun, ‘the old woman’ — a figure who appears, gives the hero exactly what he needs, and is never explained.

sentences.t: Darauf gab sie ihm ein Mäntelchen und sprach „wenn du das umhängst, so bist du unsichtbar und kannst den zwölfen dann nachschleichen.“
sentences.l: Thereupon she gave him a little cloak and said, “if you hang that about you, then you are invisible and can creep after the twelve.”
sentences.i: Thereupon she gave him a little cloak and said, “when you throw that round you, you are invisible and can creep after the twelve.”
sentences.n: “umhängen” is to hang a thing about oneself; a cloak in German is put on by hanging rather than by pulling on. “nachschleichen” takes the dative — to creep after someone. “den zwölfen” is the numeral used as a noun in the dative plural.

sentences.t: Wie der Soldat den guten Rath bekommen hatte, wards Ernst bei ihm, so daß er ein Herz faßte, vor den König gieng und sich als Freier meldete.
sentences.l: When the soldier had got the good counsel, it grew earnest with him, so that he took a heart, went before the king and presented himself as a suitor.
sentences.i: Once the soldier had this good counsel, the thing turned earnest with him, so that he took heart, went before the king, and offered himself as a suitor.
sentences.n: “es wird Ernst” is a fixed impersonal phrase: the matter becomes serious, one really means to go through with it. “wards” is ward es. “ein Herz fassen” is to take heart. “Rath” keeps the 1857 -th- (modern Rat).

sentences.t: Er ward so gut aufgenommen wie die andern auch, und wurden ihm königliche Kleider angethan.
sentences.l: He was as well received as the others too, and royal clothes were put on him.
sentences.i: He was as well received as the others had been, and royal clothes were put on him.
sentences.n: The second clause has nothing in front of its verb (“und wurden ihm königliche Kleider angethan”), which throws the weight onto the clothes. “anthun” is the 1857 spelling of antun, to put clothing on someone.

sentences.t: Abends zur Schlafenszeit ward er in das Vorzimmer geführt, und als er zu Bette gehen wollte, kam die älteste und brachte ihm einen Becher Wein:
sentences.l: In the evening at bedtime he was led into the antechamber, and when he wanted to go to bed, the eldest came and brought him a cup of wine:
sentences.i: In the evening at bedtime he was led into the outer room, and when he was about to go to bed, the eldest came and brought him a cup of wine:
sentences.n: “zu Bette” keeps the old dative -e inside a fixed phrase. “das Vorzimmer” is the room lying in front of another — the same place the kings’ sons were given, though the tale used a different word for it then.

sentences.t: aber er hatte sich einen Schwamm unter das Kinn gebunden, ließ den Wein da hineinlaufen, und trank keinen Tropfen.
sentences.l: but he had bound a sponge under his chin, let the wine run into it there, and drank not a drop.
sentences.i: but he had tied a sponge under his chin, let the wine run down into it, and drank not a drop.
sentences.n: “Schwamm” here is the noun der Schwamm, a sponge — spelled exactly like schwamm, ‘swam,’ from schwimmen, which is a different word altogether. “hineinlaufen lassen” is to let something run in.

sentences.t: Dann legte er sich nieder, und als er ein Weilchen gelegen hatte, fieng er an zu schnarchen wie im tiefsten Schlaf.
sentences.l: Then he lay himself down, and when he had lain a little while, he began to snore as if in the deepest sleep.
sentences.i: Then he lay down, and when he had lain a little while, he began to snore as though in the deepest sleep.
sentences.n: “sich niederlegen” — German makes lying down a thing one does to oneself. “fieng an” is the 1857 spelling of fing an, from separable anfangen.

sentences.t: Das hörten die zwölf Königstöchter, lachten, und die älteste sprach „der hätte auch sein Leben sparen können.“
sentences.l: That the twelve king’s daughters heard, laughed, and the eldest said, “he might just as well have spared his life.”
sentences.i: The twelve king’s daughters heard it and laughed, and the eldest said, “he might have spared his life as well.”
sentences.n: Fronting the object (“Das hörten die zwölf …”) is ordinary German and simply puts what they heard first. “der” at the head of her speech is a demonstrative used of a person, and it is dismissive: ‘that one.’ The eldest is the hard voice of this tale from here to the end.

sentences.t: Danach standen sie auf, öffneten Schränke, Kisten und Kasten, und holten prächtige Kleider heraus:
sentences.l: After that they got up, opened cupboards, chests and boxes, and fetched out splendid clothes:
sentences.n: “Kisten und Kasten” is a set alliterating pair meaning everything one has stored away; German likes such doublets and no fine distinction is intended between the two words. “herausholen” is separable.

sentences.t: putzten sich vor den Spiegeln, sprangen herum und freuten sich auf den Tanz.
sentences.l: decked themselves out before the mirrors, sprang about and looked forward to the dance.
sentences.i: decked themselves at the mirrors, skipped about, and looked forward to the dance.
sentences.n: “sich putzen” is to make oneself fine, to preen. “sich freuen auf” is specifically to look forward to something still to come, as against “sich freuen über,” to be glad of something already there. The subject is still the sisters, and German simply carries the verbs on without repeating it.

sentences.t: Nur die jüngste sagte „ich weiß nicht, ihr freut euch, aber mir ist so wunderlich zu Muthe: gewiß widerfährt uns ein Unglück.“
sentences.l: Only the youngest said, “I do not know — you are glad, but I am so strangely in mind: some misfortune will surely befall us.”
sentences.i: Only the youngest said, “I do not know; you are all so pleased, but I feel so strange: some misfortune will surely come upon us.”
sentences.n: “mir ist … zu Muthe” is impersonal with the dative — literally ‘to me it is so strange in mind,’ i.e. I feel so strange; “Muthe” keeps the 1857 -th-. “widerfahren” is to befall someone and takes the dative. “freut” here is second person plural, ihr freut euch.

sentences.t: „Du bist eine Schneegans,“ sagte die älteste, „die sich immer fürchtet.
sentences.l: “You are a snow-goose,” said the eldest, “who is always afraid.
sentences.i: “You are a silly goose,” said the eldest, “always frightened of something.
sentences.n: “Schneegans” is literally a snow goose, and it is used as an insult for a girl thought silly and timid; the literal line keeps the bird, the idiomatic one gives what the word does. The relative clause “die sich immer fürchtet” hangs on the goose.

sentences.t: Hast du vergessen wie viel Königssöhne schon umsonst dagewesen sind?
sentences.l: Have you forgotten how many kings’ sons have already been here for nothing?
sentences.i: Have you forgotten how many kings’ sons have already been here to no purpose?
sentences.n: “umsonst” is ‘in vain, for nothing.’ “dagewesen sind” is the perfect of dasein, ‘to have been here’ — the sisters’ way of not saying what became of them.

sentences.t: dem Soldaten hätt ich nicht einmal brauchen einen Schlaftrunk zu geben, der Lümmel wäre doch nicht aufgewacht.“
sentences.l: the soldier I should not even have needed to give a sleeping-draught; the lout would not have woken up anyway.”
sentences.i: I need not even have given the soldier a sleeping-draught; the lout would not have woken up in any case.”
sentences.n: “hätt” is clipped hätte. “brauchen … zu geben” — brauchen with zu means ‘to need to,’ and negated it gives ‘need not.’ “Lümmel” is a lout or oaf, said with contempt. Naming the drink aloud is the eldest sister’s one mistake, and the man on the bed is awake.

sentences.t: Wie sie alle fertig waren, sahen sie erst nach dem Soldaten, aber der hatte die Augen zugethan, rührte und regte sich nicht, und sie glaubten nun ganz sicher zu sein.
sentences.l: When they were all ready, they first looked to the soldier, but he had shut his eyes, stirred and moved not at all, and they now believed themselves to be quite safe.
sentences.i: When they were all ready, they looked first to the soldier; but he had his eyes shut and neither stirred nor moved, and they now believed themselves quite safe.
sentences.n: “erst” here is ‘first of all,’ before anything else. “die Augen zuthun” is to close the eyes (1857 spelling of zutun). “rührte und regte sich nicht” is a fixed pair of near-synonyms, which English matches with ‘neither stirred nor moved.’

sentences.t: Da gieng die älteste an ihr Bett und klopfte daran: alsbald sank es in die Erde, und sie stiegen durch die Öffnung hinab, eine nach der andern, die älteste voran.
sentences.l: Then the eldest went to her bed and knocked on it: at once it sank into the earth, and they climbed down through the opening, one after another, the eldest in front.
sentences.i: Then the eldest went to her bed and knocked on it, and at once it sank into the ground; and they went down through the opening one after another, the eldest leading.
sentences.n: “daran” is da- + an, ‘on it.’ “alsbald” is an elevated old word for ‘at once.’ “hinabsteigen” is to climb down, away from where the speaker stands. Nothing whatever is explained about the bed; the tale opens the ground and goes on.

sentences.t: Der Soldat, der alles mit angesehen hatte, zauderte nicht lange, hieng sein Mäntelchen um und stieg hinter der jüngsten mit hinab.
sentences.l: The soldier, who had watched it all, did not hesitate long, hung his little cloak about him and climbed down along behind the youngest.
sentences.i: The soldier, who had watched the whole of it, did not hesitate long; he threw his little cloak round him and went down behind the youngest.
sentences.n: “mit ansehen” is to look on at something as it goes on. “hieng … um” is umhängen in the 1857 spelling (modern hing um). “stieg … mit hinab” stacks two particles: mit, along with them, and hinab, down.

sentences.t: Mitten auf der Treppe trat er ihr ein wenig aufs Kleid, da erschrack sie und rief „was ist das? wer hält mich am Kleid?“
sentences.l: In the middle of the stair he trod a little on her dress; at that she took fright and called, “what is that? who is holding me by the dress?”
sentences.i: Halfway down the stair he trod a little on her dress; at that she took fright and cried, “what is that? who is holding me by the dress?”
sentences.n: “jemandem aufs Kleid treten” is the dative of the person with the accusative of the thing: he trod to her on the dress. “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak, from erschrecken in its intransitive sense.

sentences.t: „Sei nicht so einfältig,“ sagte die älteste, „du bist an einem Haken hängen geblieben.“
sentences.l: “Do not be so simple,” said the eldest, “you have got caught on a hook.”
sentences.i: “Do not be so foolish,” said the eldest; “you have caught on a hook.”
sentences.n: “hängen bleiben” is to get caught or snagged. “einfältig” is simple in the sense of foolishly credulous. This is the first of three warnings the eldest explains away, and the tale counts them.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie vollends hinab, und wie sie unten waren, standen sie in einem wunderprächtigen Baumgang, da waren alle Blätter von Silber, und schimmerten und glänzten.
sentences.l: Then they went the rest of the way down, and when they were below, they stood in a wondrous-splendid tree-walk; there all the leaves were of silver, and shimmered and glittered.
sentences.i: Then they went the rest of the way down, and when they were at the bottom they stood in a marvellously splendid avenue of trees, where all the leaves were of silver and shimmered and glittered.
sentences.n: “vollends” is ‘the rest of the way, right to the end.’ A Baumgang is Baum plus Gang — a tree and a passage one walks along — so a walk with trees on either hand; the hyphenated ‘tree-walk’ in the literal line keeps that shape visible.

sentences.t: Der Soldat dachte „du willst dir ein Wahrzeichen mitnehmen,“ und brach einen Zweig davon ab: da fuhr ein gewaltiger Krach aus dem Baume.
sentences.l: The soldier thought, “you will take yourself a token along,” and broke a twig from it: at that a mighty crack shot out of the tree.
sentences.i: The soldier thought, “I had better take a token along with me,” and broke a twig off it; at that a mighty crack burst from the tree.
sentences.n: He addresses himself as “du” while thinking — something German does constantly and English does not, which is why the idiomatic line says ‘I.’ “sich etwas mitnehmen” has the dative sich, ‘for oneself.’ A Wahrzeichen is a token brought back as proof, and three of them and a cup will end the tale.

sentences.t: Die jüngste rief wieder „es ist nicht richtig, habt ihr den Knall gehört?“
sentences.l: The youngest called out again, “it is not right; did you hear the bang?”
sentences.i: The youngest cried out again, “something is wrong — did you hear that bang?”
sentences.n: “es ist nicht richtig” is a set phrase for something being not as it should be, uncanny. “Knall” is a sharp report — the same sound the sentence before called a Krach, a crack.

sentences.t: Die älteste aber sprach „das sind Freudenschüsse, weil wir unsere Prinzen bald erlöst haben.“
sentences.l: But the eldest said, “those are joy-shots, because we shall soon have delivered our princes.”
sentences.i: But the eldest said, “those are guns fired for joy, because we shall soon have delivered our princes.”
sentences.n: Freudenschüsse are salutes fired in celebration; the hyphenated ‘joy-shots’ keeps the German compound visible in the literal line. “erlösen” is to redeem or release someone from an enchantment — the first hint that the princes below are under a spell, which the last sentence of the tale will confirm.

sentences.t: Sie kamen darauf in einen Baumgang, wo alle Blätter von Gold, und endlich in einen dritten, wo sie klarer Demant waren:
sentences.l: They came thereupon into a tree-walk where all the leaves were of gold, and at last into a third, where they were clear diamond:
sentences.i: Then they came into an avenue where all the leaves were of gold, and at last into a third, where they were of clear diamond:
sentences.n: “wo alle Blätter von Gold” leaves the verb out — German drops a repeated “waren” without ceremony, and English has to supply it from the clause before. “Demant” is an older High German word for diamond (modern Diamant), not a dialect form.

sentences.t: von beiden brach er einen Zweig ab, wobei es jedesmal krachte, daß die jüngste vor Schrecken zusammenfuhr: aber die älteste blieb dabei, es wären Freudenschüsse.
sentences.l: from both he broke off a twig, at which it cracked each time, so that the youngest started with fright: but the eldest stuck to it that they were joy-shots.
sentences.i: from both he broke off a twig, and each time it cracked so that the youngest started with fright; but the eldest kept to it that they were guns fired for joy.
sentences.n: “wobei” is wo- + bei, ‘at which.’ “dabei bleiben” is to stick to what one has said. “wären” is subjunctive because the eldest’s claim is reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: Sie giengen weiter und kamen zu einem großen Wasser, darauf standen zwölf Schifflein, und in jedem Schifflein saß ein schöner Prinz,
sentences.l: They went further and came to a great water; on it stood twelve little boats, and in each little boat sat a handsome prince,
sentences.i: They went on and came to a great water, on which lay twelve little boats, and in each little boat sat a handsome prince,
sentences.n: “darauf” is da- + auf, ‘on it.’ German has boats stand on the water where English has them lie. “Schifflein” is the diminutive of Schiff, and the tale keeps to it throughout: these are small craft.

sentences.t: die hatten auf die zwölfe gewartet, und jeder nahm eine zu sich, der Soldat aber setzte sich mit der jüngsten ein.
sentences.l: they had been waiting for the twelve, and each took one to himself, but the soldier got in with the youngest.
sentences.i: they had been waiting for the twelve, and each took one in with him; but the soldier got in with the youngest.
sentences.n: “die zwölfe” is the numeral used as a noun — the twelve sisters. “sich einsetzen” here is simply to get in, of a boat, with “ein” as the separable particle. Getting in with the youngest is the soldier’s one piece of gentleness, and the tale makes no remark on it.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Prinz „ich weiß nicht das Schiff ist heute viel schwerer und ich muß aus allen Kräften rudern, wenn ich es fortbringen soll.“
sentences.l: Then the prince said, “I do not know — the boat is much heavier today, and I must row with all my strength if I am to get it along.”
sentences.i: Then the prince said, “I cannot tell why, but the boat is much heavier today, and I must row with all my might if I am to move it at all.”
sentences.n: The 1857 text runs “ich weiß nicht das Schiff ist heute viel schwerer” with no punctuation between the two clauses — spoken German printed as spoken. “aus allen Kräften” is ‘with all one’s might.’ “fortbringen” is to get a thing to move along.

sentences.t: „Wovon sollte das kommen,“ sprach die jüngste, „als vom warmen Wetter, es ist mir auch so heiß zu Muth.“
sentences.l: “What should that come from,” said the youngest, “but from the warm weather? I am so hot in mind myself.”
sentences.i: “What should it come from,” said the youngest, “but the warm weather? I feel so hot myself.”
sentences.n: “wovon” is wo- + von, ‘from what.’ “als” after a question of this shape means ‘other than, but.’ “es ist mir heiß zu Muth” is the same impersonal dative the youngest used earlier in “mir ist so wunderlich zu Muthe”: she is saying how she feels, not what the air is like.

sentences.t: Jenseits des Wassers aber stand ein schönes hellerleuchtetes Schloß, woraus eine lustige Musik erschallte von Pauken und Trompeten.
sentences.l: But on the far side of the water stood a fine brightly lit castle, out of which a merry music rang, of kettledrums and trumpets.
sentences.i: But on the far side of the water stood a fine castle, brightly lit, from which merry music rang out, of kettledrums and trumpets.
sentences.n: “jenseits” takes the genitive. “Schloß” here is the noun, a castle — the same spelling the tale used in its second sentence for schloß, ‘shut,’ from schließen. “woraus” is wo- + aus, ‘out of which.’ Kettledrums and trumpets together are the sound of a court, not of a village dance.

sentences.t: Sie ruderten hinüber, traten ein, und jeder Prinz tanzte mit seiner Liebsten;
sentences.l: They rowed across, went in, and every prince danced with his beloved;
sentences.i: They rowed across and went in, and each prince danced with his own;
sentences.n: “eintreten” is separable, ‘to step in, to enter.’ “seiner Liebsten” is the adjective lieb in the superlative, used as a noun: his dearest.

sentences.t: der Soldat tanzte aber unsichtbar mit, und wenn eine einen Becher mit Wein hielt, so trank er ihn aus, daß er leer war, wenn sie ihn an den Mund brachte;
sentences.l: but the soldier danced along invisible, and when one of them held a cup with wine, he drank it out, so that it was empty when she brought it to her mouth;
sentences.i: but the soldier danced along with them unseen; and when one of them held a cup of wine, he drank it off, so that it was empty by the time she raised it to her lips;
sentences.n: “mittanzen” — the “mit” is the particle, ‘to dance along with the rest.’ “austrinken” is to drink a vessel empty. This is the one moment where the invisible man is playing rather than watching, and it is what finally frightens the youngest.

sentences.t: und der jüngsten ward auch angst darüber, aber die älteste brachte sie immer zum Schweigen.
sentences.l: and the youngest grew afraid at that too, but the eldest always brought her to silence.
sentences.i: and the youngest grew frightened at that too, but the eldest always silenced her.
sentences.n: “der jüngsten ward angst” is the impersonal dative again: it grew fearful to her. “jemanden zum Schweigen bringen” is to make someone be quiet. Three warnings and three silencings — the tale keeps count of them as carefully as it counts the sisters.

sentences.t: Sie tanzten da bis drei Uhr am andern Morgen, wo alle Schuhe durchgetanzt waren und sie aufhören mußten.
sentences.l: They danced there till three o’clock the next morning, when all the shoes were danced through and they had to leave off.
sentences.i: They danced there until three in the morning, when all the shoes were danced through and they had to stop.
sentences.n: “durchtanzen” is another of the compounds this tale runs on — to dance a thing through, i.e. to dance holes in it. “wo” here is temporal, ‘at which point,’ not ‘where.’

sentences.t: Die Prinzen fuhren sie über das Wasser wieder zurück, und der Soldat setzte sich diesmal vornen hin zur ältesten.
sentences.l: The princes carried them back over the water again, and this time the soldier set himself down in front, beside the eldest.
sentences.i: The princes ferried them back across the water, and this time the soldier sat himself down in front, beside the eldest.
sentences.n: “fahren” is transitive here — to convey someone. “vornen” is an older form of vorn, ‘at the front.’ Sitting with the eldest is not sentiment but arithmetic: it answers the heavy boat, and it also tells the reader in advance whom he will ask for.

sentences.t: Am Ufer nahmen sie von ihren Prinzen Abschied und versprachen in der folgenden Nacht wieder zu kommen.
sentences.l: At the bank they took leave of their princes and promised to come again the following night.
sentences.n: “von jemandem Abschied nehmen” is the set phrase for taking leave of someone. “versprechen” with zu and an infinitive is to promise to do a thing.

sentences.t: Als sie an der Treppe waren, lief der Soldat voraus und legte sich in sein Bett,
sentences.l: When they were at the stair, the soldier ran on ahead and laid himself in his bed,
sentences.i: When they reached the stair, the soldier ran on ahead and laid himself down in his bed,
sentences.n: “vorauslaufen” is to run on ahead. Being invisible is worth nothing unless he is back in his place before they are, and the tale keeps the practical detail in view.

sentences.t: und als die Zwölf langsam und müde herauf getrippelt kamen, schnarchte er schon wieder so laut, daß sies alle hören konnten, und sie sprachen „vor dem sind wir sicher.“
sentences.l: and when the Twelve came tripping up slowly and tired, he was already snoring again so loudly that they could all hear it, and they said, “we are safe from that one.”
sentences.i: and when the Twelve came tripping up slowly and weary, he was snoring again so loudly that they could all hear him, and they said, “we are safe from him.”
sentences.n: “herauf getrippelt kamen” puts a participle with kommen — German says how a thing came, ‘came tripping up,’ and English happens to build it the same way. “sies” is sie es. In “vor dem sind wir sicher,” vor is the vor of protection: safe from him.

sentences.t: Da thaten sie ihre schönen Kleider aus, brachten sie weg, stellten die zertanzten Schuhe unter das Bett und legten sich nieder.
sentences.l: Then they took their fine clothes off, carried them away, set the danced-out shoes under the bed and lay down.
sentences.i: Then they took off their fine clothes, put them away, set the danced-out shoes under the bed, and lay down.
sentences.n: “austhun” is the 1857 spelling of austun, to take off clothing, with the particle at the end of the clause. “die zertanzten Schuhe” is the tale’s own title-phrase turning up here in the middle of the story as an ordinary piece of housekeeping.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen wollte der Soldat nichts sagen, sondern das wunderliche Wesen noch mit ansehen, und gieng die zweite und die dritte Nacht wieder mit.
sentences.l: The next morning the soldier would say nothing, but wanted to watch the strange doings further, and went along again the second and the third night.
sentences.i: The next morning the soldier would say nothing, but meant to see more of these strange doings, and went along again the second and the third night.
sentences.n: “das Wesen” here is not ‘being’ but ‘goings-on, doings’ — sein Wesen treiben is to carry on in a certain way. “ander” for ‘next’ once more. “mit ansehen” and “mit gehen” keep the same particle: he looks on with them, goes with them.

sentences.t: Da war alles wie das erstemal, und sie tanzten jedesmal bis die Schuhe entzwei waren.
sentences.l: There everything was as the first time, and they danced each time until the shoes were in two.
sentences.i: Everything was as it had been the first time, and each time they danced until the shoes were in pieces.
sentences.n: “entzwei” is literally ‘in two,’ used of anything broken to bits. Two whole nights are compressed into one sentence: the tale has already shown what they contain and does not repeat itself.

sentences.t: Das drittemal aber nahm er zum Wahrzeichen einen Becher mit.
sentences.l: But the third time he took a cup along as a token.
sentences.i: But the third time he took a cup away with him as a token.
sentences.n: “zum Wahrzeichen” — as proof. The twigs of silver, gold and diamond, and now a cup, make four things he can lay on a table. “mitnehmen” is separable.

sentences.t: Als die Stunde gekommen war, wo er antworten sollte, steckte er die drei Zweige und den Becher zu sich und gieng vor den König,
sentences.l: When the hour had come at which he was to answer, he put the three twigs and the cup about him and went before the king,
sentences.i: When the hour had come at which he was to give his answer, he put the three twigs and the cup in his pocket and went before the king,
sentences.n: “wo” is temporal again, ‘at which.’ “etwas zu sich stecken” is to put a thing away on one’s person, into a pocket or under a coat.

sentences.t: die Zwölfe aber standen hinter der Thüre und horchten was er sagen würde.
sentences.l: but the Twelve stood behind the door and listened for what he would say.
sentences.n: “horchen” is to listen hard, and often to listen in; the situation supplies the eavesdropping. “die Zwölfe” is the numeral used as a noun again, and by this point it is practically their name.

sentences.t: Als der König die Frage that „wo haben meine zwölf Töchter ihre Schuhe in der Nacht vertanzt?“ so antwortete er „mit zwölf Prinzen in einem unterirdischen Schloß,“ berichtete wie es zugegangen war, und holte die Wahrzeichen hervor.
sentences.l: When the king put the question, “where have my twelve daughters danced their shoes away in the night?” he answered, “with twelve princes in an underground castle,” reported how it had come about, and brought out the tokens.
sentences.i: When the king put the question, “where have my twelve daughters danced their shoes away at night?” he answered, “with twelve princes in a castle underground,” told how it had all come about, and brought out the tokens.
sentences.n: “eine Frage thun” is the older way of saying to put a question (modern stellen), and “Frage” here is the noun die Frage, not the imperative of fragen. “hervorholen” is separable, to fetch out.

sentences.t: Da ließ der König seine Töchter kommen und fragte sie ob der Soldat die Wahrheit gesagt hätte, und da sie sahen daß sie verrathen waren und Läugnen nichts half, so mußten sie alles eingestehen.
sentences.l: Then the king had his daughters come and asked them whether the soldier had told the truth, and when they saw that they were betrayed and denying was no use, then they had to confess everything.
sentences.i: Then the king had his daughters brought and asked them whether the soldier had told the truth; and when they saw that they were given away and that denying was no use, they had to confess it all.
sentences.n: “Läugnen” (1857 spelling of Leugnen) is an infinitive used as a noun, which is why it is capitalised: ‘denying.’ “hätte” is subjunctive because the question is reported. “eingestehen” is separable, to confess outright.

sentences.t: Darauf fragte ihn der König welche er zur Frau haben wollte.
sentences.l: Thereupon the king asked him which one he wanted to have for a wife.
sentences.i: Thereupon the king asked him which of them he would have to wife.
sentences.n: “welche” is the interrogative standing on its own, ‘which one.’ “zur Frau haben” is to have as a wife; the king’s proclamation at the opening of the tale is being carried out to the letter.

sentences.t: Er antwortete „ich bin nicht mehr jung, so gebt mir die älteste.“
sentences.l: He answered, “I am no longer young, so give me the eldest.”
sentences.n: “gebt” is the second person plural imperative, the respectful form used to the king. The line is dry and practical, and it is also the tale’s last word on the sisters: the one who talked away every warning is the one he asks for.

sentences.t: Da ward noch an selbigem Tage die Hochzeit gehalten und ihm das Reich nach des Königs Tode versprochen.
sentences.l: Then the wedding was held on that same day, and the kingdom promised him after the king’s death.
sentences.n: “selbig” is an older word for ‘the same, that very’ (modern derselbe). “des Königs Tode” puts the genitive in front of its noun and keeps the old dative -e. “Reich” here is the noun, the kingdom.

sentences.t: Aber die Prinzen wurden auf so viel Tage wieder verwünscht, als sie Nächte mit den Zwölfen getanzt hatten.
sentences.l: But the princes were laid under a spell again for as many days as they had danced nights with the Twelve.
sentences.n: “auf so viel Tage … als” is the ‘as many … as’ correlative. “verwünschen” is to lay under a curse or enchantment, and the word confirms what the eldest let slip about the princes being ‘delivered.’ The tale ends on the losers rather than on the wedding, and never says who enchanted them or why.

glossary.alte: alt — old (inflected: eine alte Frau); as a noun, die Alte — the old woman
glossary.ansehen: ansehen — to look at, to watch (infinitive; mit ansehen: to look on at something, separable mit-); also das Ansehen, the looking
glossary.betten: das Bett — beds (pl.; ihre Betten standen neben einander); also betten, the verb ‘to bed, to make a bed’
glossary.demant: der Demant — diamond (older High German form of Diamant)
glossary.fest: fest — fast, firmly (adverb; fest eingeschlafen: fast asleep); also das Fest, a festival
glossary.frage: die Frage — question (noun; eine Frage thun: to put a question); also frage, the imperative of fragen
glossary.freut: sich freuen — rejoice, be glad (here 2nd pl., ihr freut euch; also 3rd sg., freut sich)
glossary.fuhren: fahren — carried, ferried (3rd pl. preterite, transitive: jemanden über das Wasser fahren); also in die Höhe fuhren, ‘started up’
glossary.schlaf: der Schlaf — sleep (noun; im tiefsten Schlaf: in the deepest sleep); also schlaf, the imperative ‘sleep!’
glossary.schloß: das Schloß — castle (older spelling of Schloss); also schloß, 3rd sg. preterite of schließen — schloß … zu: shut and locked
glossary.schwamm: der Schwamm — sponge (noun); spelled the same as schwamm, ‘swam,’ from schwimmen
glossary.setzte: setzen — set, put (3rd sg. preterite, mostly with a particle at the end: setzte … hinzu, added; setzte sich … ein, got in; sich setzen, to sit down)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (weak masculine noun; here dat. sg., dem Soldaten; the plural is also Soldaten)
glossary.stieß: anstoßen — adjoined, abutted on (3rd sg. preterite; an etwas stoßen: to border on something); also stoßen, ‘to knock, bump’
glossary.treiben: treiben — to be up to, to carry on (etwas heimlich treiben: to get up to something in secret); also ‘to drive’ (a flock)
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st/3rd sg. present: ich weiß, er weiß); also weiß, the adjective ‘white’
glossary.wählen: wählen — to choose, select (infinitive; sich eine zur Frau wählen: to choose one for a wife)
glossary.zwölfe: zwölf — twelve (old inflected form used as a noun: die zwölfe, the twelve of them)
